title: Quantum error correction with global control
authors: Roberto Menta, Lindsay Bassman Oftelie, Ashkan Abedi, Francesco Cioni, Marco Polini, Seth Lloyd, Francesco Caravelli, Vittorio Giovannetti
abstract: Reaching fault tolerance means scaling qubit counts by orders of magnitude, a jump that conventional superconducting architectures cannot sustain without solving the so-called `wiring problem'. Global control sidesteps this bottleneck, but implementing quantum error correction (QEC) on previously proposed global architectures incurs extremely steep overhead costs, due to the need for separate correction procedures for the computational and auxiliary qubits that comprise the global device. We resolve this by introducing the first globally-controlled architecture with zero qubit overhead. Every physical qubit is a computational qubit, and thus, every qubit is protected under a single error correcting scheme. We identify a class of cyclic stabilizer codes realizable through global iSWAP and single-qubit gates, yielding QEC thresholds nearly seven orders of magnitude larger than previous estimates for globally-controlled arrays. We further show these thresholds improve systematically as the global architecture is augmented with a limited amount of local measurement sites, demonstrating a trade-off between wiring simplicity and fault-tolerant performance.
summary: This paper introduces a novel, globally-controlled architecture for quantum computing that solves the qubit overhead problem in Quantum Error Correction (QEC). By using global driving fields on a ring of qubits, it enables syndrome extraction circuits entirely with global gates. This approach yields significantly higher theoretical QEC thresholds compared to previous local control schemes.
main_problem: The primary challenge is achieving fault tolerance in quantum computation by overcoming hardware scaling bottlenecks, specifically addressing the 'wiring problem' associated with conventional local control architectures.
main_result: The authors propose a globally-controlled architecture that implements Quantum Error Correction (QEC) with zero auxiliary qubit overhead and achieves QEC thresholds significantly higher than previous estimates.
method: They utilize global driving fields to implement programmable pairwise exchange operations, enabling syndrome extraction circuits using only global gates for cyclic stabilizer codes.
model_or_system: The model is a homogeneous ring of N computational qubits coupled via nearest-neighbor interactions. Control is achieved through time-dependent Hamiltonian engineering that allows information routing and gate operations globally.
key_observables: QEC Threshold ($p_{th}$), Logical Error Rate, Qubit Overhead (aiming for zero).
important_parameters: Code distance ($d$), Number of qubits ($N$), Global coupling strengths ($h(t), g(t)$).
main_assumptions: The model assumes the ability to selectively activate desired interactions using global detuning, and that syndrome measurement can be sequentially performed despite the global nature of the gates.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the ring topology with global couplings, connectivity graphs showing universal computation paths, and performance plots comparing achievable QEC thresholds against physical error rates.
paper_structure: The paper develops the architecture by first establishing global control to bypass wiring limits. It then details the implementation of cyclic stabilizer codes for syndrome extraction using only global gates, culminating in threshold calculations and discussions on improving performance via local measurement sites.
why_interesting: This work provides a theoretical blueprint for scaling quantum computation by fundamentally changing how error correction is implemented—by making all qubits computational and globally addressable—which has implications for superconducting circuit design.
